items.text: NHS explains when a cough means you should seek urgent attention
items.article: Most coughs are nothing to worry about, but the NHS has guidance for when to get medical help The NHS has outlined when a cough may require urgent medical attention, as many Brits are already battling so-called winter bugs. Most coughs will resolve themselves within a few weeks and you can typically manage a cough at home with rest, plenty of fluids, and paracetamol and ibuprofen, if these painkillers are appropriate for you. There is generally no need to visit a GP if you have a cough, and NHS guidance advises you should attempt to remain at home and avoid contact with others "if you have a high temperature or you do not feel well enough to do your normal activities". If you're experiencing a cough you can also try hot lemon and honey, though honey is unsuitable for babies under one year old. You can also purchase cough syrup, cough medicine or cough sweets from a pharmacist. The NHS advises you should book a GP appointment if you have a persistent cough, which is the term used for a cough lasting three weeks or more. You should also consult a doctor if you have a cough and are losing weight unintentionally, or if you have a weakened immune system. items.article: 'We all need to be doing it' for the rest of the year TV's Dr Amir Khan has taken to social media to issue an important reminder to everyone in the UK now that the calendar has switched to October. He stressed the importance of one thing everyone should now consider taking to boost their health during the winter. As the nights start to come earlier and sunrises get later, Brits will be exposed to less daylight each day. The ITV regular and practising GP took to Instagram to stress the importance of taking a vitamin D supplement to make up for what people are losing out on naturally. He said: "This is your annual October reminder to start taking your Vitamin D supplement. I know it's really sunny today, but we don't get enough sunlight between October right through to the end of March. So start taking your supplement, 400 international units or 10 micrograms, that's what the NHS recommends." Dr Khan adds that "everyone should be doing [this]", claiming that some people may need higher-than-average doses if they are already deficient. He said: "We all need to be doing it. Honestly, it will really help keep you healthy through the winter." It is important to speak to your doctor first before starting any new supplements to ensure they are suitable for you, especially if you are taking certain medications. items.text: Switching jobs, staying relevant: The Gen Z way
items.article: This article is authored by Anuradha PS, professor, CHRIST University, Bangalore. Switching jobs frequently was regarded as a blemish on the career for generations. A long service was an indication of commitment, reliability and professional maturity. The traditional career path was one that would go up, up and away and would start at the bottom, gain experience, progress up the ladder and finally retire from the organisation. It's a model that is being challenged by Gen Z. India's young people are joining a workforce where technologies, skills and even roles can evolve quicker than conventional promotion cycles. So, their eagerness to move on to new jobs doesn't necessarily equate with impatience. It might become more of a way to remain employable, more and more. The distinction matters. The Randstad 2025 global study of 11,250 people from 15 markets revealed that on average Gen Z employees had tenure of 1.1 years over the first five years of their careers, while millennials and Gen X had tenures of 1.8 years and 2.8 years, respectively. But the research shows that this mobility is largely motivated not only by dissatisfaction, but by a search for growth and development as well. It is the same in the Indian labour market. Randstad's report on the 2025 India revealed that over half of the surveyed Gen Z and millennials indicated that they would be looking to switch jobs, with the top reasons being career development and work-life balance. items.text: 'Like a dog fight': Gory rise of Bare Knuckle Boxing where 90% of bouts end in knockouts…and the plan to lure Tyson Fury
items.article: THE crack of bone on bone is followed by blood - lots of blood. The two gloveless warriors in the small triangular ring throw carefully aimed... THE crack of bone on bone is followed by blood – lots of blood. The two gloveless warriors in the small triangular ring throw carefully aimed punches at each other. In the front row, watching this brutal duel, sits Tyson Fury, transfixed by the bloody spectacle. The Gypsy King may have his sights set on Anthony Joshua and their long-awaited fight in Cardiff in December but after that, this carnival of carnage may be where he plies his trade. The Sun can reveal that Tyson is seriously considering offers to take part in the sport, which is one of the fastest growing and most ruthless spectacles in the world. Tyson hinted at an interest in switching when he was a ringside guest at a recent tournament in Miami. Bare Knuckle Boxing (BKB) CEO David Tetreault reveals initial talks have already taken place with the Fury camp. “I have had conversations with Spencer Brown [Tyson’s manager],” confirms David.

items.key: ai:inside the 'scariest house on rightmove' - as creepy home sells at auction for £200,000
items.text: Inside the 'scariest house on Rightmove' - as creepy home sells at auction for £200,000
items.article: The three bedroom detached station house in Bleasby, Nottingham , dates back to the 1840s and was listed at a guide price of £75,000 but sold on Monday for £200,000. A derelict 'house of horrors' dubbed the 'scariest on Rightmove' has been sold at auction for almost triple its guide price. The three bedroom detached station house in Bleasby, Nottingham , dates back to the 1840s and was listed at a guide price of £75,000 - but sold on Monday for £200,000. The listing promotes the property as 'a rare opportunity to acquire a substantial detached residence occupying an exceptionally large plot' and 'offers enormous potential for renovation'. But unusual photos reveal its unsettling atmosphere, with a creepy doll stood up in the corner of a room that has nicotine tar all over the yellowing walls. In the second bedroom the pink striped wallpaper is falling off the walls and a stray old fashioned metal pram is left behind in the room. Other rooms show shadowed corners, dimly lit rooms, mold all over the walls and windows boarded up.

items.key: ai:what will the world really look like when robots are doing everything for us?
items.text: What will the world really look like when robots are doing everything for us?
items.article: Forget Carson...robots will be the butlers of the future Published: 10:00, 13 September 2026 | Updated: 10:16, 14 September 2026 I f you’re the sort of person who looks to the future with hope, and thinks that AI might be the solution to all our problems, then this might be the book for you. At the same time, if you regard the arrival of AI with all the enthusiasm you had previously reserved for nuclear oblivion, then this might be the book for you as well. It’s simultaneously an optimistic peer into the crystal ball and a dire warning as to what might be to come. Scenes like this are still a while away... Joel Levy has degrees in molecular biology and psychology and has written more than 40 books, mainly of popular science. Here he has his futurologist’s hat on, and his book focuses on what the future might hold for you as you go about your daily life a few years or decades from now. Levy thinks it might be 15-30 years before we are breakfasting with robots , in the sense of having a robot butler taking care of all our breakfasting needs. As Levy puts it, ‘as long as a human can do the job better for less money, robots will not thrive’. In the future, though, it is hoped that ‘for some elements, such as its hands and fingers, the butler could deploy fluidic artificial muscles in soft-fabric housing’. There’s a lot of this sort of writing, which probably means something to someone, somewhere. Breakfast with Robots is available now from the Mail Bookshop
